content: 1. Individuals caught with drugs intended for personal use are referred to a dissuasion board instead of facing prosecution and potential incarceration. 2. An independent study conducted in 2008 revealed that the number of drug users receiving treatment increased from 23,654 in 1998 to 38,532 in 2008. 3. Between 2000 and 2008, the annual number of new HIV cases among drug users decreased from 907 to 267, a reduction attributed to the expansion of harm reduction services. 4. Contrary to initial predictions, there was no significant increase in drug use. Instead, evidence showed reductions in problematic drug use, drug-related harms, and overcrowding in the criminal justice system. 5. Community organizations play a critical role in addressing stigma and discrimination while improving access to services. 6. The organization Agência Piaget para o Desenvolvimento, established in 2004, works with vulnerable populations to improve access to healthcare, employment, and education, aiming to empower these groups and strengthen social cohesion. 7. Their outreach team, GIRU Barcelos, focuses on harm reduction efforts for heroin and cocaine users and sex workers in northern Portugal. 8. Through their initiatives, discrimination against drug users, including by healthcare professionals, has been reduced via regular meetings, mediation efforts, debates, and a local radio program called GIRU Conversations. 9. The inclusion of a peer educator and the active involvement of people who inject drugs are central to the program's interventions and are considered vital to its success. 10. In 2012, CARUSEL launched an advocacy project to raise awareness among the National Agency for Roma (NAR) and other Roma NGOs about the vulnerabilities, stigma, and discrimination faced by Roma drug users. 11. CARUSEL’s advocacy strategy includes disseminating key human rights and public health messages, conducting training sessions, collecting data through field visits, engaging community leaders, and supervising activities. 12. Roma drug users are actively involved in all project activities, and a scholarship program supports young people in attending the Roma Harm Reduction Summer School to develop outreach and advocacy skills. 13. As a result, NAR and other Roma NGOs have become more understanding of drug use within the Roma community, leading to greater acceptance of drug users. 14. Roma NGOs now provide financial support to CARUSEL for harm reduction supplies and technical expertise in reporting human rights violations against drug users. 15. The needs of Roma drug users, including culturally appropriate harm reduction activities, are now addressed in the national anti-drug strategy and action plans. 16. The Karnataka Health Promotion Trust (KHPT) has been addressing HIV prevention among sex workers for over a decade, with a particular focus on combating violence against this community. 17. KHPT collaborates with law enforcement and justice officials to raise awareness about the realities faced by sex workers and advocates for their protection and access to services. 18. Partnerships with KHPT have led to the State’s Women and Child Welfare Department making services addressing violence against women available to sex workers. 19. Community-based organizations in 30 districts work with sex workers to inform them of their rights. 20. Legal literacy training for sex workers has been developed and conducted by the Alternative Law Forum and the National Law School of India. 21. The Centre for Advocacy and Research has conducted media advocacy and trained sex workers as media spokespersons to share their experiences of violence, resilience, and actions to address these issues. 22. Red de Mujeres Trabajadoras Sexuales de Latinoamérica y el Caribe (RedTraSex), a regional network founded in 1997, advocates for the rights of female sex workers in Latin America and the Hispanic Caribbean. 23. RedTraSex seeks legal recognition of sex work, elimination of violence against sex workers, repeal of criminalizing legislation, and engagement with judicial and public officials to address the challenges faced by sex workers. 24. Since 2012, RedTraSex has worked to reduce the vulnerability of female sex workers to HIV through a regional strategy supported by the Global Fund. 25. National organizations led by female sex workers coordinate activities within countries, while sub-regional units provide additional technical support. 26. Training programs for female sex workers enhance their knowledge and capacity for HIV prevention and advocacy, while also strengthening national partners’ abilities in program coordination, policy review, and legal framework development. 27. RedTraSex ensures community participation in decision-making processes and raises awareness among stakeholders, including law enforcement and healthcare providers, about gender issues and sex work. 28. Communication campaigns aim to influence public opinion, reduce stigma, and address violence against sex workers. 29. Monitoring and evaluation of program activities are conducted at national and regional levels, measuring impacts on community attitudes, policy changes, and legal reforms. 30. Over 30,000 female sex workers from 14 countries were reached by RedTraSex activities in 2013, though stigma and lack of regulation continue to fuel violence and police aggression. 31. RedTraSex advocates for government accountability and the establishment of sex work regulations to protect female sex workers across the region. 32. Kimara Peers, a community-based NGO in Dar es Salaam, implements HIV prevention programs for young adults (18–25 years) engaged in sex work. 33. Kimara Peers also offers income-generating projects to help participants supplement or transition away from sex work. 34. Nearly 1,000 participants have been involved in these initiatives since 2007, learning about health, self-management, and financial literacy. 35. Groups of participants save together and can take small loans to fund income-generating projects, such as selling snacks, raising poultry, or working as hairdressers. 36. Participants work collaboratively on project design and resource management, demonstrating commitment to group goals and participating in weekly progress meetings. 37. Transgender Education and Advocacy (TEA) raises awareness and advocates for the human rights of transgender individuals, addressing discrimination, abuse, and health issues through legal and policy channels. 38. TEA’s advocacy goals include official recognition of transgender individuals’ names and gender identity in official documents, development of national guidelines on gender reassignment, and anti-discrimination policies. 39. TEA builds the capacity of transgender individuals to advocate for their rights, take on leadership roles, and confront challenges in public health and social service settings. 40. TEA educates the transgender community on avoiding risks, adopting healthier lifestyles, and strengthening family connections. 41. TEA’s interventions have increased self-confidence among transgender individuals, reduced cases of sexual violence and exploitation, and supported the development of gender reassignment guidelines in Kenya. 42. The Link Up project improves sexual and reproductive health and rights for young people living with or affected by HIV by increasing access to integrated services. 43. Link Up trains service providers to address stigma and better meet the needs of at-risk young people, involving young community members in training material review and session facilitation. 44. The program emphasizes service integration, gender, sexuality, and stigma reduction, with young people sharing their experiences to impact providers’ understanding and comfort levels. 45. Link Up is led by the International HIV/AIDS Alliance and partners with organizations like the ATHENA Network and Marie Stopes International to implement its programs. 46. The NewGen Asia leadership course, developed by Youth LEAD, builds capacity among young key population leaders to address HIV vulnerability and advocate for change. 47. The curriculum includes participatory activities to enhance leadership, advocacy, and public speaking skills, with over 200 participants trained across Asia and the Pacific. 48. The Indonesia National AIDS Commission has adopted NewGen to train peer educators nationwide, integrating it into the Link Up program. 49. New community networks of young key populations have been established in several countries, using social media to maintain connections and sustain advocacy efforts.
